title: In a World Bank randomized trial in Benin City, six weeks of Microsoft Copilot (GPT-4) English tutoring in nine public schools raises assessment scores 0.31 standard deviations
summary: In a World Bank randomized trial in Benin City, six weeks of teacher-guided Microsoft Copilot (GPT-4) tutoring raised scores 0.31 standard deviations overall and 0.23 in English.
account: A six-week after-school program ran in June and July 2024 in nine public schools in Benin City, Nigeria, chosen for their computer labs. First-year senior secondary students, typically 15 years old, who expressed interest were randomized: 657 to treatment and 671 to control. Of these, 422 and 337 finished the final assessment. Treated students attended up to two 90-minute sessions a week (twelve in total). They used Microsoft Copilot, powered by GPT-4 at the time, as a virtual English tutor in curriculum-aligned activities guided by teachers. In a World Bank blog post of 18 September 2024, members of the study team report that 800 first-year senior secondary students attended the after-school classes. In a World Bank blog post of 9 January 2025, the study team describes the gain as about 0.3 standard deviation. World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11125 (May 2025) is by De Simone, Tiberti, Barron Rodriguez, Manolio, Mosuro and Dikoru. It gives the months of the program and no exact days. The authors report a 0.31 standard deviation improvement on an assessment covering English, AI knowledge and digital skills, and 0.23 standard deviation on English. They equate the gains to 1.5 to 2 years of business-as-usual schooling. Effects were larger for female students and those with higher initial performance. In an article published on 23 October 2026 in Education Sciences, Sánchez-Trujillo and colleagues from Peru and Colombia report a secondary analysis of the trial. They have no tie to the World Bank team. They found an overall effect of 0.310 standard deviation (95% confidence interval 0.176 to 0.444) and 0.238 in English, and they report that the interaction with digital access was negative but imprecise.
purpose: Copilot was used as a virtual tutor to improve English learning outcomes. The measured gain is that purpose.

The reported 0.31-SD endpoint combines English, AI knowledge, and digital skills; the English-only estimate is 0.23 SD. The intervention combines extra instruction, teachers, computers, and AI, and school-year equivalents are a conversion rather than directly observed years of learning.

fields.summary: In a World Bank randomized trial in Benin City, six weeks of teacher-guided Microsoft Copilot (GPT-4) tutoring raised scores 0.31 standard deviations overall and 0.23 in English.
fields.account: A six-week after-school program ran in June and July 2024 in nine public schools in Benin City, Nigeria, chosen for their computer labs. First-year senior secondary students, typically 15 years old, who expressed interest were randomized: 657 to treatment and 671 to control. Of these, 422 and 337 finished the final assessment. Treated students attended up to two 90-minute sessions a week (twelve in total). They used Microsoft Copilot, powered by GPT-4 at the time, as a virtual English tutor in curriculum-aligned activities guided by teachers. In a World Bank blog post of 18 September 2024, members of the study team report that 800 first-year senior secondary students attended the after-school classes. In a World Bank blog post of 9 January 2025, the study team describes the gain as about 0.3 standard deviation. World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11125 (May 2025) is by De Simone, Tiberti, Barron Rodriguez, Manolio, Mosuro and Dikoru. It gives the months of the program and no exact days. The authors report a 0.31 standard deviation improvement on an assessment covering English, AI knowledge and digital skills, and 0.23 standard deviation on English. They equate the gains to 1.5 to 2 years of business-as-usual schooling. Effects were larger for female students and those with higher initial performance. In an article published on 23 October 2026 in Education Sciences, Sánchez-Trujillo and colleagues from Peru and Colombia report a secondary analysis of the trial. They have no tie to the World Bank team. They found an overall effect of 0.310 standard deviation (95% confidence interval 0.176 to 0.444) and 0.238 in English, and they report that the interaction with digital access was negative but imprecise.
